articles.title: What Happens When AI Writes Your Code but Nobody Reviews the Architecture?
articles.excerpt: AI coding tools have changed the way software gets built. Developers can now generate APIs, database schemas, authentication flows, UI components, background jobs, integrations and even entire applica…
articles.body: AI coding tools have changed the way software gets built. Developers can now generate APIs, database schemas, authentication flows, UI components, background jobs, integrations and even entire application features in a fraction of the time it previously took. For startups, founders and development teams, this is a significant advantage. But there is a problem that doesn't always appear during development. AI can generate code that works today without necessarily building a system that remains maintainable tomorrow. When teams focus entirely on shipping features and nobody reviews the underlying architecture, the application can gradually become difficult to maintain, extend, debug and scale. The problem isn't that AI writes bad code.
articles.author: DupleRevive

articles.excerpt: Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code. QuickDial is no…
articles.body: Disclosure: I'm the developer of the app described here, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working from the project's source code. QuickDial is not affiliated with WhatsApp LLC or Meta. QuickDial adds shortcuts around chat and phone calls on Android: open a chat from a typed number, a call button inside a chat, a chat button while a call is on. Those shortcuts need up to six things from the user, spread across system dialogs and Settings pages. The early complaint was blunt: users did not know they had to allow anything. The fix was not more screens. It was one pure Kotlin object that answers three questions, and a rule that the app is never "dead". A snapshot in, a plan out No Android classes go in.

articles.title: 'Flutter App Development Cost in 2026: An Honest Breakdown'
articles.excerpt: Short answer: a Flutter app for iOS and Android costs roughly $6,000–$40,000 with a South Asian developer and $25,000–$150,000 with a US agency for a simple to medium app, and $35,000–$375,000 for a c…
articles.body: Short answer: a Flutter app for iOS and Android costs roughly $6,000–$40,000 with a South Asian developer and $25,000–$150,000 with a US agency for a simple to medium app, and $35,000–$375,000 for a complex one. It takes about 250–450 hours for a simple app, 600–1,000 for a medium app and 1,400–2,500+ for a complex one. One Flutter codebase usually costs less than two native apps. Try the free app development cost calculator for your own range. “How much will my app cost?” is the first question almost every founder asks, and the honest answer is “it depends.” That answer is useless on its own, so this post breaks it down. You will get the main things that drive cost, real hourly rates by region with sources, three example scopes priced out, and the running costs that show up after launch.

articles.body: Writing complex mathematical formulas by hand in raw LaTeX slows down lecture notes, homework solutions, and technical papers—especially when formulas already live on whiteboards, PDFs, or handwritten notes. I built AI Equation Editor on AIMath to bridge visual formula editing and AI-assisted LaTeX conversion in the browser. What it does Visual Equation Editor & Live Preview : Compose fractions, integrals, matrices, Greek symbols, and multi-line equations visually with instant LaTeX rendering. Natural Language to LaTeX : Describe an equation in plain text (for example, the quadratic formula or a matrix equation) and turn it into editable LaTeX.

articles.title: Android just had one of its worst quarters, and Apple is benefiting
articles.excerpt: Android just recorded its lowest-ever share for a third quarter, with Apple's iOS bucking the trend.
articles.body: TL;DR Android accounted for 74% of global smartphone sales in Q3 2026, down five points from a year ago and its lowest-ever share for a third quarter, per Counterpoint Research. iOS climbed to a record Q3 share of 21% as iPhone sales grew year-on-year, even as the overall market shrank 16%. HarmonyOS held at 5% globally and took 22% of China’s market, with HUAWEI growing 12% while China’s market shrank 10%. The memory shortage has been dragging down phone sales all year, and new data shows it may be hurting Android more than its rivals. According to Counterpoint Research , global smartphone sales fell 16% year-on-year in Q3 2026, a sharper drop than the 11% decline seen in Q2. Android’s share of those sales slipped to 74%, down from 79% in Q3 2025.

articles.body: It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp? Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters.
